0.8 Explore which sensors were used, how many participants were assigned to it

A few things to note: - 180119 and 159005 cover the bulk of participants (371 and 517) — results will be heavily influenced by these two sensors - 159435 and 180021 have very few participants assigned (4) — these are likely on the geographic periphery of the study area

Limitations: exposure assignment was constrained to 6 sensors, with the majority of participants assigned to just 2 sensors — which reduces spatial variability in exposure estimates.

Our data is such that administrative codes are not equal to spatial units. Many conglomerados values appear in multiple sectors. Some appear in 2 sectors. Some appear in 3 or 4 (e.g. 128,409, 480)… conglomerado is NOT globally unique.

We have this hierarchy: -District: Puente Piedra -Sector (5 levels) -Conglomerado (reused within district, overlaps across sectors).. a local code system, not a globally unique cluster ID

Requires TWO-WAY clustering or a composite ID derives from sector + conglomerado

2.14 Sensor zone comparison table to show descriptively whether zones with higher PM2.5 tend to have worse cognitive scores

# No dose-response pattern is observed between PM2.5 and cognitive decline. Among the four sensors with adequate sample size (Ventanilla n=19 and Carab n=4 are too small), the highest-PM2.5 zone (Comas, 40.1 µg/m³) has the lowest rate of cognitive decline (9.3%) and the highest RUDAS scores (11.3), while the lowest-PM2.5 zones cluster around 16% decline. This is an ecological confounding artifact: the bulk of participants are assigned to just two sensors — MiPeru (n=501) and PuenteP Estadio (n=361) — which cover most of the study area and show nearly identical PM2.5 values (~32–34 µg/m³). There is effectively no meaningful exposure gradient across participants. The sensor zones are not exchangeable populations, and any apparent association between sensor-assigned PM2.5 and cognition reflects compositional differences between zones rather than a pollution effect. This demonstrates why naive ecological exposure assignment produces misleading results, and motivates future work using personal or indoor exposure monitoring.

This table is a valuable finding — it demonstrates why naive ecological exposure assignment produces misleading results, and motivates future work with better exposure characterization; a methodological lesson

2.15 Add in SES level

No statistically significant associations were observed between any sensor-assigned environmental exposure (PM2.5, PM10, temperature, humidity) and cognitive outcomes in adjusted models. Forest plot estimates for the binary cognitive decline outcome were: PM2.5 OR 0.91 (95% CI 0.75–1.11, p=0.370), PM10 OR 0.90 (95% CI 0.74–1.11, p=0.333), temperature OR 1.08 (95% CI 0.90–1.30, p=0.406), humidity OR 1.07 (95% CI 0.90–1.27, p=0.469). Continuous outcome models for RUDAS and ACE were similarly null across all four exposure variables.

2.16 Highways

The study area runs along what looks like a major highway corridor (the blue trunk road running north-south). Our participant points are clustered along and near this road. The red/pink dementia cases don’t obviously cluster in one spot, but proximity to that trunk road varies meaningfully across participants — unlike the PM2.5 values which barely vary at all.

Meaningful continuous variation from 9 meters to 4.6 km. - Median 674m — half of the participants live within ~674m of a major road - Some very close (9m) — essentially on the road - Max 4.5km — good spread at the far end - Right-skewed (mean 1001 >> median 674m) — confirms the need to log-transform

## # A tibble: 2 × 5
##   near_road_500m pct_dc mean_rudas mean_ace     n
##   <lgl>           <dbl>      <dbl>    <dbl> <int>
## 1 FALSE            16.4       23.9     78.1   682
## 2 TRUE             12.2       23.9     80.2   384

This is the most interesting result yet.

Participants living within 500m of a major road have lower rates of cognitive decline (12.2% vs 16.4%) and higher cognitive scores (RUDAS 8.29 vs 6.82, ACE 80.24 vs 78.1) — the opposite of what would be expected if road proximity were harmful. This mirrors the ecological confounding pattern seen with PM2.5: proximity to urban infrastructure in this peri-urban Lima context likely reflects better access to services, healthcare, and economic opportunity rather than greater pollution burden.

In adjusted models, road proximity was not significantly associated with the binary cognitive decline outcome (OR 1.07, 95% CI 0.93-1.24, p=0.33) or with RUDAS scores in older adults (β -0.45, 95% CI -1.35-0.45, p=0.32). The only statistically significant finding was for ACE in younger adults: each unit increase in log-distance from a major road was associated with a 0.92-point decrease in ACE score (β -0.92, 95% CI -1.65 – -0.28, p=0.005). The direction of this effect – farther from roads associated with worse cognition – is counterintuitive from a pollution-harm perspective and instead consistent with urban access advantages accruing to those living closer to major road infrastructure.

Why only younger adults? ACE has a higher ceiling and greater sensitivity than RUDAS, and younger adults (30–59) have more cognitive reserve and score variance — making subtle environmental gradients detectable where RUDAS in older adults cannot resolve them. Older adults’ scores may already reflect age-related decline that obscures any road proximity signal.

The direction of the ACE effect — farther from roads associates with worse cognition — points to urban access as the operative mechanism in this setting, not traffic-related pollution.

3 Re-run models

##                      outcome       model estimate conf.low conf.high p.value
## 1      DC binary (clustered) without SES    1.072    0.930     1.237   0.336
## 2 DC binary (SES, clustered)    with SES    1.041    0.902     1.201   0.583
## 3          RUDAS (clustered) without SES    0.069   -0.403     0.542   0.775
## 4     RUDAS (SES, clustered)    with SES    0.195   -0.288     0.678   0.430
## 5            ACE (clustered) without SES   -0.924   -1.565    -0.283   0.005
## 6       ACE (SES, clustered)    with SES   -0.785   -1.403    -0.166   0.013

In adjusted models, road proximity is null for both the binary outcome (OR 1.07 without SES, OR 1.04 with SES, both p>0.33) and RUDAS in older adults (β −0.45 without SES, β −0.30 with SES, both p>0.30). SES does not meaningfully change either null result.

For ACE in younger adults, the road proximity effect attenuates modestly after SES adjustment (β −0.92 without SES vs β −0.78 with SES) but remains statistically significant (p=0.013). SES accounts for roughly 15% of the original effect estimate — consistent with the descriptive finding that lower-SES participants tend to live slightly farther from major roads — but does not explain it away. The association remains statistically significant after SES adjustment (β −0.785, 95% CI −1.40– −0.17, p=0.013). The association between greater distance from major roads and lower ACE scores in 30–59 year olds is robust to socioeconomic adjustment.

This pattern suggests the road proximity effect in younger adults is not simply a proxy for SES, though both urbanization and socioeconomic resources likely operate through related pathways — access to healthcare, education, and economic opportunity — in this peri-urban Lima context.

3.1 The storyline for the chapter:

  1. PM2.5 — null, insufficient spatial variability. Only 6 sensors cover the study area; most participants are assigned to just two, with a PM2.5 range of roughly 32–40 µg/m³ across all zones. There is no dose-response relationship. The apparent inverse pattern (highest-PM2.5 zone has best cognition) is an ecological confounding artifact reflecting population heterogeneity across sensor zones, not a protective effect of pollution.

  2. Distance to road — significant for ACE in younger adults, robust to SES adjustment. The β attenuates from −0.92 to −0.78 after controlling for SES level, but remains significant (p=0.013). SES is a strong independent predictor of cognition across all outcomes, but explains only ~15% of the road proximity effect, indicating the two operate through partially overlapping but distinct pathways.

  3. Consistent interpretation across both exposures — urbanization as confounder. Both findings tell the same story: in peri-urban Lima, living closer to roads and higher-pollution urban centers correlates with better, not worse, cognitive outcomes. Structural access — to healthcare, education, economic resources — likely dominates any pollution effect at the exposure levels and spatial resolution available in this study.

  4. Methodological implication. Future studies in similar peri-urban settings require personal or residential-level exposure monitors, fine-grained SES adjustment, and larger sensor networks to disentangle pollution effects from the urbanization gradient. The current findings are best framed as a demonstration of ecological confounding and the limits of sensor-assigned exposure, rather than evidence of null pollution effects per se.

Implication — future studies need personal, granular exposure monitors + SES adjustment to disentangle pollution from access; indoor air monitoring

In road-type stratified sensitivity analyses, the inverse association between road proximity and ACE scores in younger adults was consistent for trunk (β −0.87, p=0.048) and secondary roads (β −0.83, p=0.007), suggesting the pooled result is not attributable to any single road classification. The primary road estimate was in the opposite direction but did not reach statistical significance (β +1.15, p=0.081), possibly reflecting the distinct spatial distribution of primary roads in this peri-urban context.

# Quick diagnostic visualization Super important: my exposure assignment is sensor-based, so if covariates cluster by sensor, it suggests potential spatial confounding (e.g., SES or age differences by neighborhood).

Some sensors do have longer upper tails. - GEOHealth_Carab_VictorRaulHT → slightly older median (~52–53) - GEOHealth_Ventanilla_NSBelen → slightly younger (~45–47)

No covariate differs significantly across sensor zones (all p > 0.05). This means sensor-zone exposure assignment is not systematically confounded by who lives where — age, SES, education, civil status, etc. are distributed comparably across zones, strengthening our argument.

the NA in the df column for chi-square is expected; it happens because we used simulate.p.value = TRUE, which runs a Monte Carlo permutation test instead of the standard asymptotic chi-square. The simulated version doesn’t return degrees of freedom. Potential footnote: p-values estimated via Monte Carlo simulation (B = 2000) due to small expected cell counts in some zones.

Add to manuscript: To assess potential spatial confounding, we tested whether key sociodemographic and health covariates differed across sensor zones using chi-square tests (categorical variables) and Kruskal-Wallis tests (continuous variables). No significant differences were observed (all p > 0.05; Supplementary Table X), suggesting that exposure assignment was not systematically associated with participant characteristics.

3.23 SES by sensor-assigned PM2.5

SES was not meaningfully associated with sensor-assigned PM2.5 (mean PM2.5 was essentially stable across NSE groups: ~33.3 to 33.6 μg/m3), confirming that SES does not confound the PM2.5 null result.
